prize_parts.citation: For the development of ionizable lipid nanoparticles for the delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles are a chemical discovery in the full sense: the design rests on lipid self-assembly, pKa-controlled charge, bilayer versus non-bilayer phase behaviour and controlled mixing kinetics, and it was turned into a general platform that carries nucleic acids into cells. The idea of a lipid that is neutral in circulation and charged in the acidic endosome is a molecular-level design principle, not just a formulation trick. It is also the one candidate on the shortlist whose clinical consequences are already large and independently validated (patisiran, the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines), and Aili and I placed it first independently of each other, from the soft-matter and the peptide/biointerface sides. I judge this configuration to be the best-supported way to recognise physical chemistry of self-assembled matter acting on medicine.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that the 2023 Medicine prize already honoured the mRNA application, so a chemistry prize can look like a second prize for the same vaccines. The second is credit: six credited names (Cullis, Madden, Hope, MacLachlan, Anderson, Langer) cannot be reduced to three without leaving out serious contributors, and my own trio (Cullis, Madden, Hope) favours the early Vancouver encapsulation and ionizable-lipid work over the later lipid-library and siRNA-clinical work that Anderson, Langer and MacLachlan represent. As a lipid physical chemist I may also overvalue the formulation chemistry relative to the later clinical development.

responses.point: Aili ranks B062 first as the enabling delivery chemistry, with rational pKa-tuned lipid design, and proposes Cullis, Anderson and MacLachlan; he regards the overlap with the 2023 mRNA prize as a framing issue, not a blocker.
responses.response: I agree on the ranking and on the 2023 point: the Medicine prize concerned nucleoside modification of the mRNA cargo, whereas the carrier chemistry is a separate achievement, and the citation should say so explicitly. I disagree on the trio. Replacing Madden and Hope with Anderson and MacLachlan shifts credit from the first encapsulation and ionizable-lipid concept toward later lipid-library screening and clinical translation. For a chemistry prize I would keep the credit with the people who established the formation principle, and I would welcome seeing where you think the early encapsulation work is replaceable.

responses.point: Linke ranks B027 first, as a clear mechanistic principle (induced-proximity degradation) that opens a new modality, and accepts the maturity risk because no PROTAC drug is approved.
responses.response: I agree that targeted degradation is a conceptually clean advance and I rank it as one of my alternatives. My reservation is the one you flag yourself: the PROTAC and molecular glue branches are distinct discoveries, so the citation would either split in two or favour one branch, and the clinical proof is still outstanding. Lipid nanoparticles carry that proof already. If the committee were to want B027 this year, I would ask you how you would handle Handa and the cereblon work without overcrowding the three names.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks B050 third and calls phase separation possibly premature as a chemistry prize because the physiological relevance of many condensates is still debated and overexpression artefacts are a concern.
responses.response: This is a fair maturity argument and it is the main reason I do not rank B050 first, even though I give it second place on conceptual grounds. The thermodynamics of liquid-liquid demixing is well understood in vitro; what is uncertain is which cellular condensates are truly functional liquids. I would still defend B050 as a strong alternative, since the physical-chemical framework (multivalency, sequence grammar) will survive even if some biological claims do not, but I accept that it is less settled than B062.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Pd-catalysed C-N coupling (B019) first as a method that changed how chemists everywhere build bonds, and judges the overlap with the 2010 cross-coupling prize to be acceptable.
responses.response: I agree that the Buchwald and Hartwig work is mature and the two-name attribution is clean, which is a real advantage over B062. My concern is that the 2010 prize already recognised Pd cross-coupling as a concept and the C-N reaction extends it, while lipid nanoparticles are a new area for the chemistry prize. I will not argue that synthesis is unworthy; I would ask that the committee does not treat an easy attribution as a stronger scientific case.

uncertainties: How the committee wants to divide credit among the six credited lipid nanoparticle names, and whether Hope and Madden should be kept over Anderson, MacLachlan or Langer.
Whether a chemistry prize for lipid nanoparticles reads as a repeat of the 2023 Medicine prize for nucleoside-modified mRNA.
My account of who made which formulation advance is from memory of the field and is not verified.
Whether the physiological relevance of biomolecular condensates (B050) will be settled enough in the near term to move it ahead of B062.
statement.conflict_note: Lipid self-assembly and membranes are my own research area, which gives me a scientific closeness to B062 and B050 but no personal tie to any credited person that is apparent from my profile; I am a colleague of Linke and Somfai at Lund, and no recusal issue is apparent from the provided profile.
